A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Common Corpus research work. Their text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across the substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original corpus statistics, OCR detection and correction examples, and phone-number detection results improving from 55–60% to 85% with customized Presidio patterns.

after.justification: v2 retains original corpus and curation results and adds multilingual model benchmarks, tokenizer evaluations, corpus-quality measurements, and overlap analysis.

M1.justification: The same corpus pipeline and named curation tools are retained; expanded implementation descriptions do not establish redesigned methods. However, v2 Appendix F.5 describes Celadon as fine-tuned, while v2 Section 5 retains v1's statement that it was trained from scratch. The PDFs do not resolve whether this represents a procedural change or inconsistent documentation.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluations on MultiBLiMP, XStoryCloze, and XCOPA, tokenizer testing on six languages from FLORES200 devtest, and comparisons using C4 and FineWeb data. The underlying Common Corpus coverage remains substantially unchanged; expanding its language statistics from 10 to 50 languages does not establish additional training data.

E2.justification: v2 Table 2 introduces evaluated comparisons with Gemma 3 270M/1B, XGLM 564M/1.7B, BLOOM 560M, and OLMo 1B. Figure 5 adds tokenizer comparisons with mBERT, GPT-2, SmolLM2, Llama 3.2, Qwen 3, and Gemma 3. Figure 3b also adds C4 and FineWeb to the embedding comparison; these comparisons are absent from v1.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce LM Evaluation Harness benchmarking, six document-level metrics on a 300,000-document sample, and tokenizer fertility measurement on FLORES200 devtest. These are substantial additions to the evaluation design. Newly specified training schedules for the previously described PleIAs models are documentation additions rather than evidence that their training changed.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of overlap with FineWeb's top 1,000 domains, embedding distributions relative to C4/FineWeb, document-quality distributions, and tokenizer fertility. These investigate corpus distinctiveness, composition, and tokenization efficiency beyond v1's descriptive statistics. The original segmentation and OCR case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, seed variation, confidence intervals, or formal significance-testing procedures. v2's statement that MultiBLiMP scores are 'significantly above random' is not accompanied by a statistical test or uncertainty estimate.

E6.justification: v2 adds aggregate and per-language benchmark results, including MultiBLiMP scores of 0.774/0.797 for PleIAs 350M/1.2B versus 0.762/0.799 for Gemma 3 270M/1B; several baselines score higher on XStoryCloze and XCOPA. It also adds fertility, quality, overlap, and expanded language statistics. Table 3 incorporates v1's 'Other' totals into Open Government while preserving the overall corpus totals.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, propositions, or proofs. The added descriptions of standard empirical quality metrics in Appendix G do not introduce substantive mathematical results.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains the largest fully open, multilingual pre-training corpus of approximately two trillion tokens. v2's abstract and introduction add the specific claim that models trained on it perform comparably to existing multilingual models, replacing the earlier emphasis on industry adoption without redefining the principal dataset contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting corpus distinctiveness to PDF versus HTML sourcing and explaining domain-specific quality profiles and benchmark performance. Appendix F newly identifies spurious OCRonos repetitions and limits Celadon's applicability to web text, while the explicit warning about shallow low-resource language coverage is removed. Appendix C's claim that only Gemma 3 outperforms the tokenizer is broader than Figure 5 supports.

D1.justification: v2 adds the full document schema, detailed tool architectures and annotation procedures, training sample counts, segmentation labels, and Celadon's classification-head and loss descriptions. Section 6 specifies model training schedules and 2,944/23,040 H100 hours. Deduplication and filtered PII categories are newly documented, although conflicting Celadon training descriptions limit reproducibility.

R1.justification: New Section 3 and Table 1 systematically position Common Corpus against seven datasets using domain coverage, multilinguality, sources beyond web crawls, and open licensing. ROOTS, DCAD-2000, FineWeb 2, and evaluation-related references expand the discussion. The earlier Impact section and associated adoption references are removed; bibliographic updates to retained works are not substantive additions.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: composition tables move to an appendix, main-text curation descriptions are condensed while appendix explanations expand, and the Impact section and development-history appendix disappear. Dedicated Related Work and Evaluation sections replace the earlier emphasis on adoption, alongside extensive prose editing and revised author information.

P2.justification: v2 adds a treemap, quality-distribution plots, tokenizer panels, a dataset comparison table, and aggregate/per-language benchmark tables. The map is redrawn with a 10,000-document threshold instead of 1,000, and the t-SNE display gains external corpora. Composition tables are relocated, and the language table expands from 10 to 50 languages with document and word counts.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's lack of direct quantitative model validation through multilingual benchmarks, detailed language-level results, tokenizer comparisons, and corpus diagnostics. Expanded metadata and curation documentation also substantially improve assessability and reuse. Conflicting tool-training descriptions and the overstated tokenizer claim weaken precision, but do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support and documentation.
